paper_title: RynnVLA-Latent: Scaling Robotic Manipulation Foundation Models with 3D-Grounded Latent Actions

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Scaling vision-language-action (VLA) models is constrained by scarce action-labeled demonstrations and incompatible control spaces across robot embodiments. We present RynnVLA-Latent, a framework that turns heterogeneous interaction videos into scalable supervision for robot policy pretraining. At its core, RynnLAM learns continuous, 3D-grounded latent actions from visual transitions without requiring native robot controls. By combining residual future-feature prediction, camera-compensated 3D-flow supervision, and camera-motion decoupling, RynnLAM encourages representations that capture control-relevant motion rather than appearance changes alone. We apply RynnLAM to 30.1K hours of human, robot, and simulation videos, producing 745.52M latent-action descriptors. RynnVLA-Latent then learns to predict latent-action chunks from visual observations and language through flow matching, before adapting its pretrained backbone and action expert to embodiment-specific robot actions. The resulting 4B policy achieves 98.8% success on LIBERO, 84.7% on LIBERO-Plus without benchmark-specific adaptation, 51.9% average success across five VLABench tracks, and 88.6% average success on the RoboTwin 2.0 bimanual benchmark. It also achieves the highest observed success rates among the compared methods on six real-world manipulation tasks across dexterous-hand and mobile-gripper platforms. Together with representation ablations and data-scaling results, these findings demonstrate the potential of latent-action supervision for scaling robot policy learning beyond native action-labeled data.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Large-scale pretraining has enabled broad capabilities in language and vision-language models (Brown et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022; Kaplan et al., 2020; Achiam et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2022; Bai et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026a). Recent vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action models extend this approach to robot control (Black et al., 2024; Intelligence et al., 2025; Bjorck et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026b; Ye et al., 2026; Yuan et al., 2026b; Bi et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026d). Scaling policy learning, however, requires supervision that connects visual observations and task instructions to actions across diverse embodiments Zhao et al. (2026a, 2025). Robot demonstrations are expensive to collect, and their native controls differ in dimensions, coordinate frames, and semantics (Zhao et al., 2026b,c). Human and web videos provide much broader interaction coverage but lack corresponding robot commands. These sources cannot simply be pooled under one native-action prediction objective. shared supervision interface is needed to exploit their visual transitions before adapting policy to particular robot. Latent actions provide such an interface by encoding changes between observations without native control labels (Ye et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025c; Bu et al., 2025b; Gao et al., 2026, 2025; Schmidt and Jiang, 2024; Chen et al., 2024). Existing approaches demonstrate the value of transition reconstruction and feature-space prediction, but visual change can include camera motion, static appearance, and effects unrelated to the agents control. representation that reconstructs images well therefore need not be equally useful for predicting low-level manipulation actions. We address this through geometric supervision and explicit camera-motion separation. We introduce RynnLAM, which encodes frame pair into motion tokens, global action latent, and camera latent. Residual futurefeature prediction preserves transition information through the bottleneck, while camera-compensated 3D-flow pseudo-labels and contrastive feature warping encourage motion-sensitive representations. Camera-pose prediction and gradient reversal further encourage separation of ego-motion from manipulation-related cues. These objectives provide geometric grounding without requiring manually annotated robot actions; they encourage camera decoupling rather than guaranteeing exact viewpoint invariance or physical identifiability. Using RynnLAM as an offline labeler, we construct shared latent-action supervision for 25 video sources spanning human interaction, real robots, and simulation. The corpus contains approximately 30.1K hours and 3.057B frames and yields 745.52M latent-action descriptors. We then pretrain RynnVLA-Latent, Mixture-of-Transformers policy that couples pretrained vision-language backbone with narrow action expert. The policy predicts latent-action chunks from multi-view observations and language via flow matching, without native-action or proprioceptive supervision. In robot post-training, we reuse both the backbone and action-expert trunk, introduce proprioception, and retarget the output projection to native robot commands. This separates video-based motion supervision from embodiment-specific action alignment. Our evaluation follows the same path from representation learning to robot deployment. On LARY, frozenrepresentation probes test whether the descriptors predict low-level control targets, with the full descriptor achieving average relative-action MSE 0.38. After native-action post-training, the 4B policy obtains 98.8% on LIBERO, 84.7% on LIBERO-Plus, 51.9% average success across five VLABench tracks, and 88.3% average success under the RoboTwin 2.0 Native protocol. These benchmarks respectively assess task execution, perturbation robustness, semantic grounding, and bimanual manipulation. Six real-world tasks on stationary dexterous and mobile gripper platforms test the interface after adaptation to different controls. Data-scaling and component studies further characterize where the approach helps and where performance remains limited. Our contributions are as follows: 3D-grounded latent-action supervision. We introduce RynnLAM, which combines residual feature prediction, camera-compensated 3D-flow supervision, and camera-motion decoupling to construct continuous transition representations without native robot-action labels. Scalable VLA pretraining from heterogeneous video. We develop RynnVLA-Latent, which learns shared latent-action targets from 30.1K hours of human, robot, and simulation videos, and transfers the pretrained policy to native robot controls through embodiment-specific post-training. Representation and policy-level validation. We demonstrate control predictability through frozen-representation probes, competitive manipulation performance across simulation and real-world platforms, and improvements with increasing latent-action pretraining data.

sections.title: 2.1 Latent Action Learning
sections.content: Latent action learning provides way to exploit videos without native action annotations by representing the transformations between observations. LAPO (Schmidt and Jiang, 2024) and Genie (Bruce et al., 2024) demonstrate that latent action spaces can support policy learning and controllable prediction from unlabeled videos. LAPA (Ye et al., 2025) learns discrete latent actions through frame-transition reconstruction and uses them as VLA pretraining targets, while Moto (Chen et al., 2025c) learns motion tokens for autoregressive pretraining and transfers the resulting motion priors to robot control. IGOR (Chen et al., 2024) similarly compresses image-goal transitions into shared action representations for learning across human and robot videos. These approaches establish visual transitions as scalable source of action-like supervision beyond robot demonstrations. Subsequent work investigates how to make such representations more useful for control. UniVLA (Bu et al., 2025b) introduces language-guided, task-centric latent actions in DINO feature space, while villa-X (Chen et al., 2026) augments visual reconstruction with proprioceptive forward-dynamics objective to ground latent actions in robot states and actions. Latent actions also serve as transferable conditioning signals for world models: AdaWorld (Gao et al., 2025) uses video-derived latent actions for adaptable future prediction, and DreamDojo (Gao et al., 2026) learns continuous proxy actions from large-scale human videos. Garrido et al. (Garrido et al., 2026) further investigate constrained continuous latent actions for representation-space world modeling on in-the-wild videos. Our focus is the geometric grounding of latent actions without robot-native action or proprioceptive supervision. RynnLAM combines residual future-feature prediction, camera-compensated dynamic 3D-flow supervision, and contrastive feature warping to learn factorized continuous transition representation. dedicated camera-pose pathway and an adversarial objective further encourage separation of camera ego-motion from manipulation-relevant motion. Rather than relying on continuity or feature-space prediction alone, these complementary objectives encourage the latent representation to capture physical scene changes and provide shared supervision across human, simulated, and real-robot videos.

sections.title: 2.2 Vision-Language-Action Models
sections.content: Vision-language-action (VLA) models transfer pretrained vision-language knowledge to robot control. OpenVLA (Kim et al., 2024) and FAST (Pertsch et al., 2025) explore action-token prediction, while π0 (Black et al., 2024), GR00T N1 (Bjorck et al., 2025), Xiaomi-Robotics-0 (Cai et al., 2026), and LingBot-VLA (Wu et al., 2026) couple vision-language backbones with continuous action generators. Open X-Embodiment and RT-X (ONeill et al., 2024), together with π0.5 (Intelligence et al., 2025), demonstrate the value of cross-embodiment and heterogeneous training. To handle incompatible action spaces, UniAct (Zheng et al., 2025) learns universal action representations with embodiment-specific decoding, X-VLA (Zheng et al., 2026) uses soft prompts and domain-specific projections, and Qwen-RobotManip (Yuan et al., 2026a) aligns canonical state-action representations and camera-frame motion. Human videos provide additional supervision through latent-action labels in GR00T N1 (Bjorck et al., 2025) and reconstructed hand motion in VITRA (Li et al., 2025). Our work focuses on constructing shared supervision interface for scalable VLA pretraining, rather than aligning heterogeneous native control parameterizations. RynnVLA-Latent learns continuous RynnLAMgenerated latent-action chunks from human, robot, and simulation videos through flow matching. The same descriptors also condition cross-embodiment video generation in the companion RynnWorld-Latent model. Native robot actions and proprioception are introduced only during embodiment-specific post-training, allowing large-scale video-based pretraining to be separated from executable control alignment.

sections.title: 3 RynnVLA-Latent
sections.content: A central obstacle to scaling robotic manipulation is that the most abundant sources of manipulation knowledgehuman videos, web videos, simulation, and heterogeneous robot datasetsdo not share common action representation. We address this problem by learning shared latent-action space supervised by visual transitions and geometric pseudo-labels, without requiring identical native control spaces. This latent space serves both as an automatic annotation for large-scale unlabeled video and as an intermediate control representation that can later be aligned with concrete robot actions. Our framework consists of three components. We first assemble and preprocess the multi-embodiment video corpus (Sec. 3.1). We then train RynnLAM (Sec. 3.2) with future-feature prediction, dynamic 3D-flow supervision, and camera-motion decoupling, and use its encoder to label the corpus offline. Finally, we train RynnVLA-Latent (Sec. 3.3), vision-language-action policy that learns to generate these latent actions from visual observations and language via flow matching. sections.title: 3.3 RynnVLA-Latent
sections.content: The latent actions produced by RynnLAM provide an embodiment-agnostic interface between video understanding and control; Fig. 4 summarizes the resulting training pipeline. Because the same encoder maps heterogeneous videos into common descriptor layout, human, robot, and simulation videos can contribute to one policy objective without reconciling their native action conventions. Building on this interface, RynnVLA-Latent separates the learning of generalizable manipulation dynamics from embodiment-specific action alignment. During pre-training, the policy learns to generate latent actions from raw observations and language; during post-training, the same flow-matching objective is retargeted from latent actions to the target robots action space. This decoupling allows the model to scale on unlabeled multi-embodiment videos, while requiring costly action-labeled demonstrations only for the final embodiment alignment. Architecture. RynnVLA-Latent adopts Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architecture (Liang et al., 2024) that couples pretrained vision-language model with narrow action expert. The VLM backbone, RynnBrain (Li et al., 2026a), jointly encodes multi-view images and the language instruction into causal prefix. The action expert is randomly initialized transformer stream with the same depth as the VLM but smaller hidden width. At each layer, tokens from the two streams are jointly attended, while their output projections and feed-forward pathways remain separate. The VLM prefix remains causal and cannot attend to the action suffix, whereas the action suffix is bidirectional and attends to the full VLM prefix. This design allows the action expert to exploit rich visual-language context without duplicating the full VLM capacity, and permits action-prediction gradients to refine the VLM representation. We instantiate RynnVLA-Latent with 2B and 4B VLM backbones while keeping the action expert narrow. The 2B and 4B names refer to the backbone variants; total policy parameter counts, including the action expert, are reported in Tab. 2. Pre-training: flow matching on latent actions. Both the VLM and the action expert are updated. This stage requires neither robot actions nor proprioception; its supervision is available for any video from which RynnLAM can extract latent actions. Multi-view conditioning. Embodiments differ not only in action spaces but also in camera configurations. To avoid hard-coding fixed set of views, RynnVLA-Latent organizes latent-action generation using canonical camera slots. For each present view, its VLM patch embeddings are pooled into slot token and prepended to the action expert. Empty slots are masked in attention and in the loss. This slot-based interface accommodates samples with different available views without supervising absent outputs. Camera configurations are mapped to the canonical slots; the interface alone does not guarantee invariance to an unseen viewpoint. Post-training: embodiment-specific action alignment. Pre-training yields model that generates embodimentagnostic latent actions but does not yet produce executable robot commands. In post-training, we retarget the same flow-matching objective from RynnLAM latents to the target robots action space and fine-tune the full model on demonstrations from that embodiment. Proprioceptive state is introduced only at this stage. No separate action decoder is added: the readout trunk pretrained during pre-training is retained and terminated by thin newly initialized projection to the target action dimension, so the experts pretrained capacity is reused rather than duplicated. We use unified action layout and mask dimensions not used by the target embodiment, allowing one interface to support different robots. Inference. At inference, RynnVLA-Latent initializes the output sequence from Gaussian noise and integrates the learned velocity field from τ =1 toward τ =0 using Euler steps. In pre-training this output is latent-action chunk; after post-training it is directly the robot action chunk. The VLM prefix is computed once and reused across integration steps. The resulting action chunk is executed in full before replanning. Post-training updates the policy parameters and changes the prediction target to native actions while retaining this sampling procedure; execution requires no separate latent-to-action decoder.

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: We evaluate the proposed framework from three complementary perspectives. First, we assess the quality of the latent action representation itself, asking whether RynnLAM learns representation that is predictive of low-level control signals rather than merely encoding visual semantics or appearance change. Second, we report completed downstream policy evaluations on simulation benchmarks covering manipulation success, robustness to perturbations, and language grounding. We additionally evaluate bimanual manipulation on RoboTwin 2.0 under the Native protocol. Third, we evaluate post-trained policies on real-world dual-arm platforms with different end-effectors and mobility, testing applicability across these deployment settings after embodiment-specific adaptation.

sections.title: 4.3 Latent Action Representation Quality
sections.content: We evaluate the quality of the learned latent representation using the LARY benchmark (Nie et al., 2026). We focus on its low-level control regression track, which decodes end-effector trajectories from frozen representation using lightweight MLP. Since the official absolute targets can be partially predicted from the currently visible robot pose under short temporal strides, we additionally report relative setting that predicts end-effector displacements from the first frame. This setting more directly measures whether the representation encodes motion rather than static pose. We compare with general semantic encoders, generative pixel encoders, embodied latent-action models, and general latent-action models, following Nie et al. (2026).

Removing motion-token residual forcing causes the largest degradation in the relative setting, increasing the average MSE from 0.38 to 0.57. Its absolute average also increases to 0.37. We therefore distinguish these controlled configuration comparisons from the full-scale results reported in Tabs. 4 and 5. Latent Actions as Cross-Embodiment Action Alignment. We compare RynnLAM-based supervision against two strategies for aligning heterogeneous action spaces: shared canonical action vector with masking (Yuan et al., 2026a; Intelligence et al., 2025) and embodiment-specific input and output projections (Agarwal et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2026). For human videos without native action labels, both explicit alignment baselines use motion-capture-derived wrist poses and fingertip positions as pseudo-action supervision, with implementation details provided in Appendix C. As shown in Tab. 9, under the same approximately 1,000-hour pretraining subset, RynnLAM-based pretraining achieves higher LIBERO-Plus success than both alternatives: 82.3% versus 80.5%/82.1% for 2B, and 84.2% versus 83.5%/83.6% for 4B. Backbone, camera slots, and latent-action targets. Under the shared training subset, the RynnBrain-based models outperform their Qwen-VL counterparts on LIBERO-Plus by 3.5 and 4.5 percentage points for 2B and 4B, respectively. Removing canonical camera slots reduces LIBERO-Plus success by 0.4 and 1.3 percentage points, while replacing RynnLAM descriptors with LAPA targets reduces it by 2.1 and 2.9 percentage points. These results support the combined design of the vision-language backbone, multi-view conditioning interface, and continuous latent-action supervision, with the most consistent differences appearing under perturbation-based evaluation. Scaling Behavior. We investigate the impact of latent-action pretraining data scale by training RynnVLA-Latent with 10%, 30%, 50%, 70%, and 100% of the video corpus and evaluating the resulting policies on LIBERO-Plus under the same downstream protocol. As shown in Fig. 8, both 2B and 4B models achieve their highest success rates with the full pretraining corpus, demonstrating an overall benefit from scaling up heterogeneous video supervision. While the 2B model improves monotonically across the evaluated data fractions, the 4B model exhibits slight decrease from 10% to 30% before improving with larger data scales. These results suggest that increasing latent-action pretraining data generally improves downstream robustness within the evaluated range, although the relationship is not strictly monotonic for every model size.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented framework for latent-action pretraining of vision-language-action policies from heterogeneous interaction video. RynnLAM combines residual feature prediction, camera-compensated 3D-flow pseudo-labels, contrastive warping, and camera-pose decoupling to produce continuous transition descriptors without native robot-action labels. RynnVLA-Latent learns to predict these descriptors through flow matching, then reuses its pretrained backbone and action expert while retargeting the output space to robot commands. The evaluation supports this interface at two levels. Frozen probes show that the descriptor is predictive of low-level controls, with average relative-action MSE 0.38 on LARY. After native-action post-training, the 4B policy achieves 98.8% on LIBERO, 84.7% on LIBERO-Plus, 51.9% average success on the five reported VLABench tracks, and 88.3% under the RoboTwin 2.0 Native protocol. It also attains the best success rate among the compared baselines on all six real-world tasks across stationary dexterous and mobile gripper platforms. Performance remains task-dependent, and RoboTwin scores remain below the strongest listed baselines. Together with the data-scaling trend, these findings support shared transition supervision as practical route to policy pretraining across incompatible control spaces. Limitations. Depth, camera poses, and flow are estimated pseudo-labels, so geometric supervision does not guarantee calibrated metric motion or complete separation of camera and manipulation information. Low-level control probes measure predictability, and decoded flow provides qualitative interpretation, rather than proof of causal action identifiability. Policy performance varies across tasks and perturbations, and deployment still requires embodiment-specific action-labeled demonstrations. The current results also do not establish general scaling law or isolate pretraining-data volume from all differences in optimization exposure. Future work will improve geometric consistency, viewpoint robustness, and transfer with less target-robot supervision.

sections.title: A Benchmark Details
sections.content: A.1 Latent Action Representation Quality We first evaluate the latent action representation itself. Rather than judging latent actions by downstream manipulation success, which entangles representation quality with the rest of the VLA stack, the LARY benchmark (Nie et al., 2026) probes the frozen representation directly. We adopt its low-level control regression track, which decodes end-effector trajectories from frozen representation through lightweight MLP action expert, scored by MSE across CALVIN (Mees et al., 2022) and VLABench (Zhang et al., 2025) (7-DoF Franka), RoboCOIN (Wu et al., 2025) (12-DoF bimanual) and AgiBotWorld-Beta (Bu et al., 2025a) (16-DoF AgiBot G1); we leave aside its semantic classification track, which scores category separability rather than physical grounding. The official targets are absolute end-effector states in fixed base frame. At the short stride (s=5) used to form each image pair, the currently visible pose can help predict these targets. Absolute-target performance may therefore reflect static pose information as well as transition information. We therefore also report relative setting that re-expresses the same targets as displacements from the end-effector state at the first frame, leaving the probe, splits, stride and metric untouched, so that the probe emphasizes displacement prediction rather than absolute pose reconstruction. We compare against three of the paradigms of (Nie et al., 2026): general semantic encoders (V-JEPA 2 (Assran et al., 2025), DINOv3 (Siméoni et al., 2025)), generative pixel encoders (Wan2.2 (Wan et al., 2025), FLUX.2-dev (Labs, 2025)), and Embodied LAMs (LAPA (Ye et al., 2025), UniVLA (Bu et al., 2025b), villa-X (Chen et al., 2026)), plus Moto (Chen et al., 2025c) and DreamDojo (Gao et al., 2026) evaluated under the identical protocol. LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus. LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023) is language-conditioned tabletop benchmark on Franka Emika Panda. Its four suitesSpatial, Object, Goal, Long, 10 tasks each with 50 human-teleoperated demonstrationsisolate spatial grounding, target disambiguation, goal following, and long-horizon chaining. We fine-tune single policy jointly across all 40 tasks and evaluate each suite over 500 rollouts (50 per task). LIBERO-Plus (Fei et al., 2025) reuses the same 40 tasks as robustness diagnostic, perturbing seven factorslayout, viewpoint, robot initial state, language, lighting, background, and sensor noiseover 10,030 curated episodes. We evaluate the LIBERO-finetuned checkpoint without additional LIBERO-Plus adaptation to measure robustness under these perturbations. VLABench. VLABench (Zhang et al., 2025) returns to fixed Franka Panda but shifts the difficulty from control to grounding: task categories spanning primitive and composite interactions, built in MuJoCo over 2,164 objects in 163 categories, with instructions written to convey intent implicitly rather than by template. We fine-tune on the benchmarks official primitive-task split and evaluate on the fixed episode sets of the benchmarks public tracks, which hold the tasks constant while varying what the policy must resolve to locate the target: in-distribution, cross-category, common-sense, semantic-instruction, and unseen-texture. We omit the benchmarks cross-task track, whose train/test partition is left to the user and whose numbers are therefore not comparable across papers. RoboTwin 2.0. RoboTwin 2.0 (Chen et al., 2025a) contains 50 bimanual manipulation tasks, including handovers, cooperative lifting, and stabilization followed by manipulation. The benchmark provides 731 object instances in 147 categories and supports multiple dual-arm embodiments. We use ALOHA-AgileX and the Native protocol, with 50 clean and 500 randomized demonstrations per task (27,500 in total). single policy is trained jointly across all 50 tasks and evaluated in clean and randomized scenes. Randomization covers clutter, lighting, background, tabletop height, and language. Because randomized demonstrations are included during training, the two evaluation domains measure performance within this training protocol rather than zero-shot transfer from clean training to randomized scenes. Results for this protocol are reported in Tab. 6.

sections.title: B Teleoperation Setup
sections.content: For Marvin-WUJI, we collect demonstrations through the teleoperation system shown in Fig. 10. The hardware setup consists of dual Tianji 7-DOF robotic arms and dual Wuji 20-DOF dexterous hands, yielding total of Figure 10 Marvin-WUJI demonstration collection. Motion trackers control the dual robot arms, and data gloves control the dexterous hands. 54 degrees of freedom. For arm control, the human operator wears five HTC Vive trackers (mounted on the chest, both wrists, and both upper arms). The system computes wrist-to-chest relative transforms at 100-120 Hz and feeds them into Pinocchio-based inverse kinematics solver running in separate process. The resulting joint commands are further smoothed by Ruckig trajectory generator with velocity, acceleration, and jerk constraints before being sent to the robot arms at 200 Hz. For hand control, the operator wears Manus data gloves. The raw glove signals are converted to 21-point MediaPipe hand skeleton format and retargeted to the 20-DOF Wuji hand joint space via dedicated retargeting module, with an exponential moving average filter applied for motion smoothing. Details of Action-Alignment Baselines To compare our latent-action-based cross-embodiment alignment with conventional action-alignment strategies, we implement two baselines commonly used in VLA pretraining. C.1 Shared Vector Representation Following prior VLA research (Yuan et al., 2026a; Intelligence et al., 2025), we map heterogeneous state and action spaces from different data sources and embodiments into unified 85-dimensional canonical vector representation. The layout is designed for dual-arm embodiments. For single-arm robots, only the first half of each bilateral slot group is populated. The vector is organized into the following semantic slots: 1. Joint Position (013): dual-arm joint positions, with 7 dimensions allocated to each arm. 2. EEF Pose (1431): Cartesian end-effector position (3 dimensions) and orientation represented using continuous 6-D rotation representation (6 dimensions) for each arm. 3. Gripper Position (3233): one gripper-position dimension for each arm. 4. Dexterous Hand (3473): 20 dimensions reserved for each dexterous hand. 5. Torso (7477): 4 dimensions for torso degrees of freedom. 6. Head (7880): 3 dimensions for head and neck motion. 7. Base (8184): 4 dimensions reserved for mobile-base degrees of freedom. Different embodiments populate different subsets of this unified vector according to their available degrees of freedom. Unused dimensions are excluded from the training loss through per-dimension binary mask, preventing spurious supervision on structurally absent action dimensions. C.2 Domain-specific Projection Following prior work (Agarwal et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2026), this variant retains shared action expert but replaces the common input and output projections with bank of domain-specific projections. Each physical robot embodiment is assigned domain identifier, which selects the corresponding projection parameters for that sample. In this design, the main policy remains shared across embodiments, while the lightweight boundary projections capture embodiment-specific differences in action parameterization and distribution. C.3 Human Egocentric Datasets For human egocentric datasets, we treat human motion as separate embodiment type when using domainspecific projections. These videos carry no native control labels; wrist poses and the positions of five fingertips are mapped to the corresponding slots of the unified vector. C.4 Delta Actions and Normalization During training, all action slots use delta-action representation: each action in an action chunk is expressed relative to the robots current state. For normalization, the 6-D end-effector rotation slots are left unchanged. All other action slots are normalized using the q0.01 and q0.99 quantiles computed from the training data. RynnVLA-Latent Dataset Video captioning. We use Qwen3-VL (Bai et al., 2025) to generate captions for the video data. Specifically, we leverage the models strong video-language understanding capabilities to produce detailed, structured descriptions of each video clip. The videos are first sampled at frame rate of 1 FPS and split into segments of 5 seconds. For each segment, we provide the following prompt to the model: Please describe this video in detail. Include the following aspects: 1. The main subject and action in the video. 2. 3. 4. The environment and background. Any objects and their interactions. The overall scene context and atmosphere. Provide concise but comprehensive caption in one paragraph. The generation is performed with maximum output length of 512 tokens and temperature of 0.7 to balance creativity and coherence. The generated captions are then collected and stored in JSON format for downstream tasks. Optical flow annotation. We employ DPFlow (Morimitsu et al., 2025), state-of-the-art optical flow estimation model. For each video, frame pairs are processed sequentially at native resolution, and the estimated flow fields are visualized via color encoding and saved as MP4 videos at 25 FPS. Depth annotation. We employ Depth Anything 3 (Lin et al., 2025), specifically the DA3NESTED-GIANTLARGE-1.1 checkpoint, which provides dense per-frame depth predictions along with camera pose estimation. Each video is sampled at 30 FPS and processed at working resolution of 392 pixels (short side, upper-bound resize).

sections.title: E Extended Ablations of RynnLAM
sections.content: To complement the main ablations, we further evaluate RynnLAM under the relative low-level control protocol of the LARY benchmark (Nie et al., 2026). We focus on the relative action setting because it reduces reliance on reconstructing the currently visible absolute end-effector pose, and thus more directly reflects whether the frozen representation encodes motion rather than static scene appearance. Tab. 10 reports the results. The first block studies training and objective variants. RynnLAM w/ 2D flow replaces the 3D scene-flow decoder with 2D appearance-flow decoder; together with the w/o 3D flow variant in the main table, it compares no-flow, 2D-flow, and 3D-flow supervision. The full 3D-flow model has lower average error than either variant; adding 2D-flow supervision does not improve over the no-flow variant, so an additional motion-prediction objective alone does not explain the gain. RynnLAM w/o contrastive feat. removes the anti-shortcut contrastive feature objective and falls back to the plain motion-weighted cosine loss, testing the utility of contrasting warped features against unchanged source features. RynnLAM w/o feat. prediction disables the future feature-prediction branch entirely, measuring how much of the representation quality is driven by next-frame feature prediction versus the latent-specific objectives. RynnLAM w/ zm from latent tokens compresses zm from the latent tokens instead of the raw target-frame features, removing the direct feature-space pathway into the bottleneck; it degrades the average MSE substantially, supporting the direct target-feature pathway for preserving information useful to the control-regression probe. The second block probes za, zc, and zm separately using the same checkpoint. Motion tokens yield the lowest average MSE among the individual components (0.54), but remain worse than the full descriptor (0.38). Thus zm carries substantial control-relevant information, while the combined descriptor gives the best average result. The global action and camera latents alone achieve 0.93 and 0.95, respectively, and are less predictive under this probe. These slice comparisons establish differences in probe utility; they do not by themselves prove complete semantic disentanglement of the representation. Together, these studies support the complete objective and the direct target-feature pathway for control regression. The component probes additionally show that the full descriptor is more predictive than any individual slice. These findings explain the choice of descriptor used for policy pretraining, while downstream evaluations separately assess its utility after adaptation to native robot controls.
